speaker: Patient
text: 63-year-old male. The patient reports noticing a skin lesion on his chest 2 months ago, which he believes has increased in size. He denies any associated pain or itching with the lesion. He has a medical history significant for type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypercholesterolemia, and glaucoma.

speaker: Doctor
text:
That is helpful; has the lesion bled, ulcerated, or developed a raised border? Also, do you use any new lotions or medications on your chest recently?

REQUEST TEST: Full skin exam with dermoscopy of the chest lesion.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: FULL SKIN EXAM WITH DERMOSCOPY OF THE CHEST LESION: Inspection reveals a single, partly elevated lesion on the chest exhibiting asymmetry, border irregularity, and varied color with a diameter larger than 6mm. Palpation confirms the lesion is firm, partly elevated, and does not change form on pinching. Skin biopsy histopathology findings show atypical melanocytes infiltrating the epidermis and dermis, confirming the diagnosis of malignant melanoma.

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Skin lesion on the chest. I also have Lesion has increased in size, Not painful, Not itchy. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Acute appendicitis and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text: I must clarify that a chest skin lesion cannot be a sign of acute appendicitis; the previous diagnosis was likely an error. Can you describe the color and texture of the lesion, and does it have an irregular or notched border? Please also tell me if you have noticed any changes in your vision recently.

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypercholesterolemia, glaucoma Social history: Smokes 1 pack of cigarettes daily for the last 40 years, drinks two to three beers on weekends

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) of the chest. The combination of a rapidly growing, painless, non-itchy lesion in an elderly male smoker with a history of diabetes and glaucoma (potential ocular involvement risk) is highly suspicious for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. I recommend immediate biopsy and an ophthalmology evaluation.
